ACYQ: Built to copy the payoff of autocallable income notes, a structured product that pays high regular income while stock markets stay above set barrier levels. The income is the draw; if markets fall through those barriers, losses can arrive quickly, so it is a specialist tool rather than a core bond holding.
AQLG: Large US companies picked for growth, meaning businesses expected to expand their earnings faster than the wider market, chosen by an active manager. Growth stocks tend to swing more than the market and shine brightest in rallies, so this plays the growth role rather than a steady core one.
ASCI: Small companies outside the US, picked one by one by an active manager, with industrial firms the biggest slice at about a third. Small overseas stocks are less followed and sometimes overlooked bargains, but they swing more and can be harder to trade than big-company shares.
BITI: A trading tool that gains when bitcoin falls, built to work for a single day at a time. Because it resets daily, holding it longer can lose money even when bitcoin ends lower, so it suits short-term bets against bitcoin rather than long-term investing.
BRIB: Intermediate-term bonds, mostly high-quality corporate debt arranged as a ladder of maturities, from companies screened by a values score for contributing to the common good. It aims for steady income and capital preservation as a portfolio's bond core, with the values screen as its twist.
DHDG: Large US stocks with a partial shield that resets every quarter: it absorbs a defined middle slice of losses over each three-month period, leaving the smallest dips and the deepest falls unprotected. The quarterly reset renews protection four times a year, far more often than most buffer funds.
EINC: North American pipeline and energy transport companies, including master limited partnerships, the firms paid to move and store oil and gas. It's an income play on energy infrastructure: the payouts are the point, and it moves with energy markets and interest rates more than with oil prices alone.
EIRL: Irish companies, with banks at about two-fifths and airlines, building materials and food firms making up much of the rest. It's a concentrated single-country fund where a few giants dominate, so it behaves more like a handful of stocks than a whole market.
FCEF: A fund of closed-end funds and other income funds from around the world, holding dividend stocks, bonds and preferred shares underneath. It's built purely for income and variety in one package, though owning funds that own funds means its costs come in layers.
FEDM: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US, tilted toward firms with stronger environmental and social scores and a lighter carbon footprint. It works as a core overseas holding, with banks and industrial companies the biggest slices and no US stocks at all.
FINT: Overseas stocks held through a basket of other funds, mixing developed and emerging markets with tilts toward quality, dividends and shareholder payouts. It works as a one-stop international holding, though the fund-of-funds design means the mix shifts as the underlying funds and their tilts change.
FLMX: Mexican large and mid-sized companies, led by food and drink makers at about a third, with miners, banks, phone companies and industrial firms behind them. It's a single-country bet closely tied to the US economy, and returns for US investors also ride on the peso.
FLSW: Swiss large and mid-sized companies, led by drug makers at about two-fifths, with banks, food and consumer brands and industrial firms behind them. It's a single-country holding built on defensive, dividend-paying giants, so it tends to hold up better than most when markets fall.
FLXN: Below-investment-grade bonds and loans, the riskier debt that companies with weaker finances issue, gathered for their higher interest payments. It's built for income, and because its borrowers are shakier, it tends to fall alongside stocks in bad markets instead of cushioning them like safer bonds.
GMOM: A fund of other funds that follows price trends worldwide, shifting money toward the stock markets, bonds and commodities rising most and pulling back from those falling. The trend approach can sidestep long slumps, but it can also be caught wrong-footed when markets reverse suddenly.
GOOW: Built entirely around Alphabet stock, using swap contracts to boost the shares' weekly move by about a fifth while paying cash out to investors every week. It's a concentrated trading tool on one company, and the weekly reset means it is not a buy-and-hold stake in Alphabet.
HECO: Companies in the digital asset world, from bitcoin miners and crypto platforms to big technology and banking names with crypto businesses. It's actively managed with a built-in hedge meant to blunt the worst drops, which sets it apart from plain crypto stock funds.
HEFT: An actively managed mix built for an era of crisis and upheaval: stock and commodity funds, managed futures and Treasury bonds, plus short bets against heavily indebted companies. It's meant to cushion a portfolio in turmoil, and it will trail plain stock funds in calm bull markets.
IAUG: Large companies in developed markets outside the US, combined with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in August, in exchange for a cap on gains. The year resets every August, so the protection left depends on when you buy.
IBHK: Corporate bonds all coming due in 2031, mixing riskier high-yield debt with bonds rated just above junk in search of extra interest. Like owning one big bond, the fund wraps up near the end of 2031, so it is designed to be held to that finish line.
IBLC: Companies tied to digital assets: crypto exchanges, bitcoin miners and the chip and data center firms that support them. It's a focused bet on the crypto economy, so it swings hard with bitcoin's mood and holds no coins of its own to steady it.
ICPY: Undervalued companies outside the US, chosen where the company's own insiders are buying shares or the firm is buying back its stock. The insider signal is the twist on plain value investing, and the mix leans toward consumer brands, banks and industrial firms overseas.
IFGL: Property companies and real estate trusts in developed markets outside the US, from Japanese developers and Australian warehouse landlords to European mall owners. It's an income-leaning bet on overseas real estate that moves with property markets and interest rates abroad, not with US housing.
ITDB: A retirement fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2030, mixing US and overseas stocks with bonds, currently a little more than half in stocks. It shifts toward bonds on its own as 2030 gets closer, putting the whole retirement glide path in one holding.
JANU: Large US stocks paired with options that absorb the first part of a fall over each year starting in January, while gains above a set level stay uncapped. Buying in the middle of the year means part of that protection may already be used up, so timing matters here.
JULU: Large US stocks paired with options that absorb the first part of a drop over each year starting in July, while gains above a set level stay uncapped rather than cut off. The year resets each July, so the protection in place depends on when you buy.
METL: Miners, explorers and royalty companies producing metals the energy build-out needs, from copper and silver to uranium, picked by an active manager. It's a focused bet on metal prices and mining shares, so it swings much more than the broad market.
MMSD: Short-term municipal bonds from states, cities and public agencies across the US, picked by an active manager. Their interest is exempt from federal income tax and the short maturities keep price swings small, so it works as a steadier parking spot for cash.
NNOV: The big growth companies of the Nasdaq, with technology about three-fifths of the mix, combined with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in November, in exchange for a cap on gains. It still swings more than a broad fund, just with a softer landing.
OBTC: A trust that holds bitcoin itself rather than futures, so its price follows the coin held in custody. It offers stock-market access to bitcoin without opening a crypto account, though as a trust it can trade above or below the value of the bitcoin it holds.
PSL: Consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of food, drinks and household basics, picked by momentum, meaning whichever of these steady stocks have been climbing most strongly. Staples are normally the market's calm corner, but the momentum tilt makes this version livelier than a plain staples fund.
QARP: Large US companies picked for being both financially strong and sensibly priced, a quality-at-a-reasonable-price approach, with technology about a quarter of the fund. The two-part screen sets it apart from plain market funds: it passes on both shaky bargains and glamorous stocks priced for perfection.
QTPI: Preferred shares and similar income securities, issued mostly by big banks and other financial companies, picked because their payouts qualify for lower dividend tax rates. It's an income holding with bond-like payments and bank-heavy risk, and preferred shares can drop sharply when credit worries flare up.
RACK: Companies that build and power data centers: memory and chip makers, electrical and cooling equipment, and the energy suppliers behind them. It's a focused bet on the artificial intelligence build-out, so it rises and falls with spending on new computing capacity.
REXC: Rare earth miners and refiners based outside China, the country that dominates supply of the metals used in magnets, motors and defense equipment. It's a narrow bet on building a separate supply chain, concentrated in a handful of small miners, so it swings hard.
RFDA: US companies chosen for dividend income across all industries, from banks and energy to technology and health care, with a dynamic approach that shifts emphasis as markets change. It aims for income with steadier growth as a core stock holding, and its rotating tilt sets it apart from plain dividend funds.
RSEE: Stock funds covering US large and small companies, developed overseas markets and emerging markets, combined and adjusted by a systematic model. It can shift toward cash-like safety when its signals turn cautious, which smooths the ride but can leave it behind in strong rallies.
RSIT: Stocks from developed and emerging markets outside the US, with a managed futures strategy stacked on top using the same money. The futures side follows trends in bonds, currencies and commodities and can make money in falling markets, smoothing the ride of the overseas stocks.
RUSC: Small US companies spread across every industry, with health care, industrials and banks the biggest slices and no single name big enough to sway the fund. Small companies can grow faster than big ones but swing harder, so this works as a growth add-on beside a core large-company holding.
SPLS: The largest US stocks, matched to the broad market, with an actively managed bond portfolio layered underneath to earn extra interest on top. The bond layer is the twist: it aims to beat a plain stock fund, but it can also drag when the bond choices miss.
SPXN: America's biggest companies with banks, insurers and real estate firms removed, leaving technology at nearly half and health care and consumer brands next in line. It's for investors who want the broad market without financial stocks, which makes it more tech-heavy and a bit jumpier.
SPYC: The largest US stocks, held through a broad market fund, with an options overlay added on top to reshape the ride. The options aim to soften sharp drops while keeping some upside in rallies, a cushion that costs a little return in calm markets.
STXK: Small US companies across all industries, weighted by company size, with technology, banks, industrials and health care the largest slices. It's a plain, broad small-company building block from a manager known for skipping social and environmental screens, and small stocks mean bigger swings than the overall market.
TAXT: Investment-grade municipal bonds from governments and public agencies across the US, paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It plays the steady income role in a taxable account, and its longer-term bonds make its price move more when interest rates change.
TIPZ: US Treasury bonds whose principal adjusts upward with inflation, spanning short through long maturities. It pays interest like other Treasury funds and is meant to protect purchasing power, though its longer bonds still fall when interest rates rise.
WDEF: European defense companies: makers of aircraft, missiles, ships, radar and military electronics, almost entirely industrial firms. It's a focused bet on Europe spending more on its own defense, so it moves with government budgets and contracts rather than the wider economy.
WINC: Bonds and loans tied to governments and companies in emerging market countries, picked by an active manager for their income. It pays more than developed-market bond funds, but adds currency swings and political risk from countries where economies and rules can shift quickly.
XBJL: Large US stocks with a speed boost and a small cushion: over each year starting in July, gains count at an accelerated rate up to a cap, while a modest buffer absorbs the first part of any loss. The doubled-up upside is the draw, and the cap limits what a huge rally pays.
YALL: Large US companies across every major industry, screened to leave out firms the manager judges to be working against American values. It's a values-based version of a core stock holding, tech-led like the broad market, where the screen matters more than stock picking.
ZMAY: Exposure to America's largest companies with a built-in shield: it is designed to protect against market losses over each one-year period that starts in May, in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms reset every May, so how much protection is left depends on when you buy.
